about: Generated by scripts/changelog.mjs from the commits of the local tree-sitter grammar repositories; used when they are not checked out. Do not edit.
author: suciui

entries.text: Regenerate the Bash parser with tree-sitter v0.25.6 instead of v0.25.10. This lowers the parser's language ABI version from 15 to 14, which makes it compatible with older tree-sitter runtimes
Heredocs can now be followed by more commands on the same line, such as `;`, `&`, `&&`, `||` or a pipeline after file redirects (for example `cat <<EOF 2>&1 | tail -1`).
A heredoc on its own, or after a file redirect, is now recognized as a valid statement.
Case statements now accept the `;&` and `;;&` fallthrough endings on the last item.
Redirects that are missing their target, such as a trailing `>`, are now recognized as incomplete redirects instead of causing a hard parse failure.
Heredoc delimiters that are partly quoted or escaped (for example `E'OF'` or `'A'"B"C`) are now read correctly, and a delimiter followed by `|`, `;` or `)` is handled.

A heredoc now ends only on a line that is exactly the delimiter. Lines that merely start with the delimiter text are treated as content, and expansions right after such a prefix are no longer skipped.
Quoted strings and escaped backslashes are handled correctly: a `$'...'` string ending in an escaped backslash, and double-quoted text inside regex patterns, no longer break parsing.
Non-ASCII characters after `{` no longer cause a crash or a misread brace expression.
Windows (CRLF) line endings are no longer included in comments.

Comparisons inside `[[ ... ]]` now parse correctly, including `=`, `==`, `!=` and `=~` against patterns, regexes and `~` paths. `!` negation and chained variable assignments are also handled correctly.
Substring expansions that use a variable as the length, such as `${var:$n}`, are now parsed, as are `{ ...; }` groups whose last command has no terminator.
Herestring redirects (`<<<`) can now be mixed with other file redirects on one command.
The test suite has new and expanded cases for commands, literals, statements and heredoc delimiters.
Extended glob groups (shopt -s extglob) at the start of a word, such as ls !(*.c) or PATTERN+=+($A|+($B)), now parse in command arguments and variable assignments.

In files with Windows (CRLF) line endings, a heredoc with an empty line right before its end word is now closed at that end word; before, the end word was read as heredoc content and the rest of the file failed to parse.
The C parser has been regenerated with a newer version of the parser toolchain. It also includes internal memory-handling updates that make parsing more robust.

Code that uses unexpanded macros now parses cleanly: macros placed before a type (storage class, memory section, inline), macros that stand for a whole statement or declaration without a semicolon, and unit-test macros that open a function body

AUTOSAR compiler-abstraction macros are recognized, including type macros with memory and pointer classes (e.g. CONST, VAR, FUNC, P2CONST) and function-pointer macros (e.g. P2FUNC, CONSTP2FUNC) in typedefs, declarations, struct fields and parameters

Code split by #if/#else/#endif parses correctly: conditional directives inside expressions or argument lists, if/else statements whose parts are cut by a directive, function headers that differ per configuration, and extern "C" blocks wrapped in #ifdef __cplusplus
Loop headers written as macros, such as "for Each_item(i)", are now recognized as loops
Files that contain only initializer-table entries, meant to be included inside a larger table, now parse without errors
Large constant tables declared with AUTOSAR type macros no longer turn into deeply nested error trees, which could crash tools walking the syntax tree
Initializer lists that contain #define lines, or that lose a comma between braced entries because of a skipped #else branch, now parse correctly
Attribute-like macros after a function's parameter list are recognized more reliably, so macro modifiers in front of a function are no longer misread as the function name
#include and #embed lines that end with trailing spaces or tabs are now parsed correctly, instead of producing errors that break the surrounding code (for example inside #if/#else blocks)

Calling-convention macros between the return type and the function name (for example `XMLPUBFUN int XMLCALL xmlInit(void);`) are now recognized in function declarations, function definitions, function-pointer typedefs and function-pointer struct members, instead of producing parse errors.

A calling convention placed after the pointer star (for example `xmlChar * XMLCALL xmlStrdup(...)`) is now parsed correctly, for both macro-based and built-in Microsoft calling conventions such as `__cdecl`.
Attribute-like macros at the end of a function prototype (for example `... LIBXML_ATTR_FORMAT(3,4);`) are now accepted, as they already were after function definitions.
Struct fields may now have macro modifiers in front of their type (for example `VX_VOLATILE VX_UINT32 count;`), the same as regular declarations.
Labels can now end a block, as C23 allows (for example `done: }`), and the parser no longer reports an error there.
Function prototypes that end with a bare attribute macro just before the semicolon (for example `void f(void) OS_ATTR_NORETURN;`) are now read as proper function declarations instead of parse errors.
Typedefs followed by an attribute-style macro call (for example `... LIBXML_ATTR_FORMAT(2,3);`) now parse correctly.
Initializer lists made of macro calls with no commas between them, often each inside its own `#if` block, now parse correctly. Normal comma-separated lists still parse the same way.
A label followed directly by a `#line` marker, as in lexers produced by generator tools, is now recognized correctly.

Embedded inline-assembly functions in the Wind River Diab style (for example `asm volatile int f(int x) { … }`) are now recognized as functions. This also works when a macro stands in for the `asm` keyword, and the assembly body is not misread as C code.
Inline assembly statements whose `asm` keyword comes from a macro (for example `OS_TOOL_ASM_KEYWORD volatile ("dsync" : : : "memory");`) are now recognized as assembly.

Variables wrapped in linker-section and alignment macros are now parsed correctly. This covers macros before or after the variable name, with or without an initial value, for example `os_syncspot_t OS_SECTION_ATTRIB_PRE(.bss.os.Lock) Lock[] OS_SECTION_ATTRIB_POST(.bss.os.Lock);`.
Macro calls can now take operators (`++`, `+=` and others), full declarations (`uint8 buf[4]`) and linker section names (`.bss.shared.os.x`) as arguments without causing parse errors.
A `#define` with several block comments in a row before a line continuation no longer ends the macro early, so the code after it is no longer misread.

Struct members written as macro calls without a semicolon (for example configuration macros like `VAR_ALIGN(T x, 32)`) are now recognized. Pointer qualifier macros placed before or after the `*` are also handled correctly.
A macro that expands to more `case` labels inside a `switch` no longer breaks parsing of the statements that follow it.
Type attributes inside `sizeof(...)`, such as `__attribute__((aligned(4)))`, are now understood.
Functions that follow several macro lines without semicolons (for example a series of generator macros) are now recognized as functions instead of being parsed incorrectly

Declarations with a linker-section macro followed by an alignment macro before the variable name (e.g. section + aligned attributes on a lock array) are now parsed correctly instead of treating the alignment macro as a function
The section name inside linker-section macros (such as ".bss.os.Lock") now appears as one argument instead of as a separate section name entry in the parse tree
A variable with a section macro after its name and an initial value (e.g. "x SECTION(.data.x) = 0") now accepts only one section macro before the "=" sign
Code with section and alignment macros around declarations parses more reliably, because the parser has fewer ambiguous ways to read these declarations

C code that writes an "if" condition as a macro call without parentheses around it (for example "if Is_front_wheel(n) { ... }") is now parsed as a normal if statement, so it no longer produces parse errors.

An assignment whose value comes from a macro that already includes the closing semicolon (for example "count = Get_counter(stage, current)" with no semicolon written after it) is now read as a complete statement, so the code that follows it parses correctly.

An #include line with stray characters after the file name (for example "#include <pstunit.h>/") no longer breaks the code that follows. The extra characters are ignored, as compilers do, and a comment after the file name is still read as a comment.

A declaration made of only a storage class and a name, without a type (old C "implicit int", for example "extern HsmDrvExtsn_LifecycleStateUpdateFlag;"), is now recognized instead of producing a parse error.
A macro call whose argument is a whole statement ending in a semicolon (for example "COU_CALL(State = 2;, "set State")") is now parsed correctly, so the code after it no longer produces errors.

AUTOSAR function declarations with a storage class and a macro keyword in front, whose parameters also use macro types (for example "extern STATIC FUNC(Std_ReturnType, X_CODE) X_Check(P2CONST(uint8, AUTOMATIC, X_DATA) Ptr, uint16 Size);"), now parse without errors.

A preprocessor line such as "#endif" inside an expression or statement that is followed by a block comment running over several lines (for example "#endif /* X */ /* PRQA S 2053" with the comment closed a few lines below) no longer breaks the rest of the function. The comment is read as part of the directive line.

A macro in front of a parameter or argument that stands for the leading parameters or arguments, comma included (for example "static uint8 CanHL_ReInit(CAN_HW_CHANNEL_CANTYPE_FIRST uint8 doRamCheck)" or "CanLL_InitEnd(CAN_CHANNEL_CANPARA_FIRST initPara)"), no longer causes a parse error.

Several macros between a type and the star of a pointer (for example "V_MEMROM1 DescSvcHead V_MEMROM2 V_MEMROM3 * pSvcHead") and a macro in front of a function pointer typedef (for example "typedef void DESC_API_CALL_TYPE (*DescPreHandler)(...)") now parse without errors.

Test macros whose argument is several words (for example "COU_ADD_SUITE(VIL__DIA__ALL Application SessionControl tests, ...)"), several statements or a loop (for example "COU_SET_BY_CALL(for (i = 0; i < 200; i++) queue[i] = 0; length = 20;, "Initialize")" or "COU_CALL_FOR(4, CLOCK = 5; MAIN(), "run")") now parse, also when such a macro is called inside another one (for example "COU_FOR(200, COU_CALL(Step(); MAIN(), "run"))").

Memory class macros around the type, after the star and in casts (for example "osqROM0 osqROM1 const osqROM2 TaskType osqROM3 * osqROM4 tab[2] = {...};" or "(osqPRAM1 osuint32 const osqPRAM2 * osqPRAM3)p") now parse without errors, and a cast takes the name just before the macro as its type.
Memory or debug macros in front of the type of a typedef (for example "typedef DBGVAR const struct S_t * S_cpot;" or "typedef BAP_IMPL_FAR void (*F)(void);") no longer cause a parse error.

A condition macro without parentheses (for example "if BSWM_ISDEF_X { ... }"), a loop macro that stands for the whole loop head (for example "for (AllClients) { ... }") and a macro call between string literals (for example ""a" M(x) "b"") now parse.
Test macros in an initializer list that bring their own comma, before a closing name (for example "{ ADD_TEST(A, B, f) ADD_TEST(A, C, g) COU_ADD_TEST_END, }"), no longer cause a parse error.

A channel macro in front of a call or an array element argument (for example "CanHL_GetTxHwToLogHandle(CAN_CHANNEL_CANPARA_FIRST Can_GetHwHandle(Htrh))"), a pointer type passed to a macro (for example "GetInterfacePointer(Request_t*, ArbReq)"), a macro call with its first argument left empty (for example "COU_CALL(, "t+1")") and a stray semicolon after a struct field now parse without errors.
A "#" with no directive name, alone on its line or right before a comment (for example "#/** @file ... */" at the top of a file), is now read as a null directive instead of causing a parse error.
A cast to type qualifiers alone, C89's implicit int (for example "(const)((T) x)"), no longer causes a parse error.

A declaration with a storage class but no type in front of an array (for example "extern suites_c_file[];"), or in front of a bare struct, union or enum ("extern struct PduInfoType_s;"), no longer causes a parse error.

A name followed by a minus and a number inside macro arguments (for example "COU_CALL_FOR(timeout-2, ...)" or "len -1") is now read as a subtraction instead of a macro modifier in front of a negative number.
A switch on a macro that expands to the parenthesized value, such as "switch Get_mode(n)", no longer causes a parse error.
A file that holds the elements of an initializer and ends in a number without a comma (for example "0/*closing element*/") no longer causes a parse error.
Unnamed bit-fields such as "unsigned int : 0;" in a struct no longer cause a parse error.
Variables placed at a fixed address with "@", such as "int x @ 0x4711;" (IAR, Cosmic, CodeWarrior), no longer cause a parse error.
An "__asm { ... }" block inside a function body, and an asm function whose body holds only plain instructions, no longer cause a parse error.
A line marker such as '# 139 "file.h"' in the middle of a declaration, as preprocessor output has, no longer causes a parse error.

A call between two macros that open and close a block, the second bringing the semicolon (Simulink's "_ssSafelyCallGenericFcnStart(S)(...) _ssSafelyCallGenericFcnEnd;"), no longer causes a parse error.
String macros written before a string literal in a call argument, such as 'fprintf(fp, INDENT LOCATION "text")', no longer cause a parse error.
A cast with a macro after the star, such as "(volatile uint16 * FAR)p", no longer causes a parse error.

Macro arguments that only a macro turning them into a string can take, such as "COU_ADD_SUITE({suite_B}, ...)", "COU_ADD_SUITE(<suite_C>, ...)" and "COU_ADD_SUITE(C++Suite, ...)", no longer cause a parse error.
Names with a byte that is not UTF-8 in them (a Latin-1 letter such as the "Ae" in a file saved as Latin-1) no longer cause a parse error; the byte is kept as part of the name.

The interrupt, register bank, trap and alignment qualifiers of the Tasking compiler, such as void _interrupt(1) _bisr_(osdSystemLevel) osDispatcher(void), void __trap_fast(0) f(void) or T x __align(4);, no longer cause a parse error.
The at-sign qualifiers of the Cosmic compiler, such as @interrupt void isr(void) or char @far *p;, no longer cause a parse error.
A Ctrl-Z character, the end-of-file mark old DOS editors leave at the end of a file, no longer causes a parse error.
A stray control character in C code, such as a 0x02 byte an old editor left after a comment, no longer causes a parse error.
A #pragma, #error or #warning line in the middle of an expression or an argument list, or after the last element of an initializer, no longer causes a parse error.

A variable whose whole head is a macro call, such as M(IF0, ST_YMR_A) = { 0xff, 0xff };, and an unnamed struct after memory class macros, such as volatile __saddr struct { UINT f:1; };, no longer cause a parse error.

A #define between alternative function heads and the function body, an initializer value that comes from an #include line, and a memory class macro before the star of a function name, such as static void MEMORY_HUGE *f(void *d), no longer cause a parse error.

Parameters with several macros around their type, such as f(NMH_FIRST V_MEMROM1 tType V_MEMROM2 event), or a macro that brings its own star, such as memcpy_sc(void SC_FAR_POINTER const s1), no longer cause a parse error.
A function pointer parameter after a type name, such as uint16 f(uint8 (*const cb)(void));, no longer causes a parse error.
Braces in comments inside an asm block, and one-line CodeWarrior assembly such as __asm JMP main;, no longer cause a parse error.
Loops whose body follows a preprocessor block, and loop heads made of macro names between commas, such as for (i = 0, All_wheels, ++i), no longer cause a parse error.

Macros in front of casts, sums and names in arguments and initializers, such as f(CHANNEL_FIRST (const T *)p), f(TP_CHANNEL_INDEX a+1), f(CONTEXT_FIRST(c) value), s.x = BIT_CAST value; or { V_MEMROM0 (V_MEMROM1 vuint8 * V_MEMROM2)0 }, a macro with its own star in a cast, such as (const void SC_FAR_POINTER)Key, and padding macros after an initializer element no longer cause a parse error.
A macro in front of a cast and a sum in an argument, such as vSetTpNew(TP_CHANNEL_INDEX (word)rub_SepTime+1, s), no longer causes a parse error.
Calls nested three or more deep inside parentheses, such as x = (A(B(C(a))));, no longer cause a parse error.
A macro in front of a qualified cast in an argument, such as f(X_FIRST (const T *)p), is now read as a macro call with the type as its argument, followed by the value.
Interpolated strings with several braces in a row, such as {{{value}}}, are now read correctly. Literal braces and the expression inside them are no longer mixed up, including in raw strings.
Pointer code in unsafe blocks now parses correctly. This covers assigning through a cast pointer, `*p++` compared with `(*p)++`, `&` applied to a method call, and member or index access on a pointer.

`async`, `partial` and `required` can now be used as ordinary variable or parameter names without breaking the surrounding code. The same fix applies to async and static lambdas and anonymous methods.

Local functions are now recognized after other statements, for example a `static` local function placed right after a method call. Local functions that name an explicit interface, such as generated `void IComponentConnector.Connect(...)`, are also recognized.

Preprocessor directives such as `#region` and `#pragma` with text containing `/`, `/*` or a trailing slash are now read correctly. An `else` branch separated from its `if` by `#if`/`#endif` is also recognized.
A `when` condition after a type pattern, as in `case int when x > 0:`, is now read as a condition and no longer as a variable name.
`ref partial struct` declarations are now supported.
CMake files containing bracket arguments or bracket comments are now parsed more reliably, because the parser no longer depends on leftover internal state from earlier parsing.
Parsing recovers more predictably after syntax errors in CMake files.
The parser tooling used for development was upgraded to a newer version.

Refreshed the prebuilt Windows x64 native parser binary (tree-sitter-cpp.node). It is a rebuild with no source or grammar changes, so users get an updated precompiled module without compiling it themselves.
Support for C++26 features: pack indexing (`Ts...[0]`), contracts (`pre(...)`/`post(...)` on functions), and `= delete("reason")`.
Support for C++23 `if consteval` / `if !consteval` blocks.
Support for pointer-to-member syntax, including `Widget::*` declarations, function pointers to members, the `->*` operator and `void (C::*)(int)` in type-ids.

Support for several more C++ constructs: `using std::a, std::b;` with several names, attributes on enum values, enum names and structured bindings, attributes before `friend`, `template class Foo<int>;` explicit instantiations, `_Static_assert`, GNU `typeof`, and Clang `_BitInt(N)`.
`extern "C" {` wrapped in `#ifdef __cplusplus` and split across preprocessor branches, as in many C/C++ headers, no longer breaks parsing of the declarations inside.
Defaulted or deleted functions defined outside their class (`A::A() = default;`, `void f(int) = delete;`) are now parsed correctly.

Preprocessor `#if`/`#ifdef` blocks inside constructor initializer lists, and macro names after a string (`"x=%" PRIu64`), are now parsed correctly. So are destructor calls on templated types (`p->~Foo<int>()`, `p->A<int>::~A<int>()`).
Parsing is more robust, because reused parse state from another language can no longer cause out-of-bounds reads in the string scanner. Test coverage was also expanded for the new constructs.
Code inside #if / #else / #endif blocks in C++ files is parsed again instead of being dropped from the syntax tree

C-only macro guesses (unexpanded macros, AUTOSAR-style function and declaration macros, macro-style loops, function headers or if/else split by #if) no longer apply to C++ code, so constructors, function calls, casts and initializers are recognized correctly
Function definitions, for loops and else branches in C++ follow standard C++ syntax again and are no longer misread as macro constructs
The prebuilt Windows (x64) parser is rebuilt to include these parsing fixes
#include and #embed directives with trailing spaces or tabs before the end of the line now parse correctly instead of producing syntax errors.
Rebuilt the prebuilt Windows x64 parser binary so it includes the corrected preprocessor directive parsing.

AUTOSAR compiler abstraction macros such as FUNC(...), VAR(...), CONST(...), P2VAR(...) and P2CONST(...) are now recognized as types in declarations, so AUTOSAR-style C++ code parses correctly instead of producing errors
Unit-test macros that open a code block at file scope, such as COU_TEST(TestCase_001, "Init") { ... }, are now recognized as test definitions
Calling-convention macros placed between a return type and a function or variable name are now accepted in declarations
Ordinary C++ constructs such as constructors, function calls, casts, "new T(...)" and conversion operators are still parsed as before and are not mistaken for the new macro forms
The prebuilt Windows (x64) parser has been rebuilt to include the new macro support

Function declarations that end with an attribute macro before the semicolon, such as "void f(void) MK_ATTR_NORETURN;" or "int g(const char *fmt, ...) ATTR_FORMAT(1, 2);", now parse as normal function declarations instead of producing errors. This also works for member function declarations inside classes.
"new" expressions that put the type in parentheses, such as "new (TData)(a, b)", now parse correctly. Placement-new forms such as "new (buf) T(1)" are still recognized.
The prebuilt Windows (x64) parser binary has been rebuilt and includes both parsing fixes.

Macro calls written on their own line without a trailing semicolon inside a function body (for example `SIM_LOCK(mutex)`) are now recognized as statements, so the code after them in the function parses correctly instead of producing errors.
An `#ifdef __cplusplus` / `#if defined(__cplusplus)` block that holds ordinary C++ code, such as a class definition, no longer breaks parsing of the lines that follow it.

The `extern "C" {` … `}` wrappers split across `__cplusplus` preprocessor blocks are now recognized even when the lines have trailing comments or blank lines after them, so the declarations between them stay ordinary top-level declarations.
Diab-style `asm` macro function definitions are now only recognized in C code and are no longer treated as a special construct in C++ code.
The prebuilt Windows (x64) parser binary has been removed from the package, so Windows users now need to build the parser from source.
C headers wrapped in `#ifdef __cplusplus` / `extern "C" {` guards now parse correctly when the opening brace is on its own line after `extern "C"`.
Those `extern "C"` guard lines now parse correctly when they end in a one-line `/* ... */` comment, for example `#endif /* __cplusplus */` or `} /* extern "C" */`, not only a `//` comment.
Added a test that checks headers using these `extern "C"` guard styles keep parsing correctly.

An "if" whose condition is a macro call without its own parentheses, for example "if Is_front_wheel(n) { ... }", is now recognized as a normal if statement, so the code after it no longer produces parse errors.

An assignment from a macro call that has no trailing semicolon, for example "count = Get_counter(stage, current)" on its own line, is now recognized as a complete statement, and the lines after it parse correctly.
Added tests to make sure both macro styles keep parsing correctly and that ordinary "if (...)" statements and normal assignments still work as before.
A comma expression inside decltype (for example "decltype(chip.SetChannels(a, b), void())", a common SFINAE pattern) no longer causes a parse error.

A file-scope declaration made of a macro call followed only by attributes (for example the OSEK "TASK(Task_10ms) __attribute__((weak));") is now read as a function declaration instead of producing a parse error.
Picks up the C grammar fixes for #include lines with stray characters after the file name and for macro calls with whole statements as arguments.

AUTOSAR declarations and functions in C++ files with a macro keyword in front of the compiler abstraction type (for example "STATIC FUNC(void, X_CODE) Init(void);" or "extern STATIC FUNC(Std_ReturnType, X_CODE) X_Check(uint8 Ptr, uint16 Size);") now parse without errors, as they already did in C files. The keyword is shown as a macro modifier and FUNC(...) as the return type.
Picks up the C grammar fix for block comments over several lines after an #if or #endif line inside code.

Picks up the C grammar fixes for macros that stand for leading parameters or arguments, several macros before a pointer star or a function pointer typedef, and test macros that take several words, statements or loops as arguments, also when nested in another macro call.

Export and memory macros in front of a built-in type or in front of a type name and a declarator (for example "ECUDLL_API char *EcuDllGetProjectName()" or "V_MEMROM0 MEMORY_ROM vuint8 kVersion = 1;") no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.

Picks up the C grammar fixes for memory class macros around types and in casts, macros in typedefs, condition and loop head macros, macro calls between strings, test macros in initializer lists and more macro argument forms.

Picks up the C grammar fixes for the null directive (a "#" with no directive name, for example "#/** @file ... */") and for casts to type qualifiers alone (for example "(const)x"): neither causes a parse error in C++ files any more.
A switch on a macro that expands to the parenthesized value, such as `switch Get_mode(n)`, no longer causes a parse error in C++ files.
`delete[] ((T *) p)` is read as an array delete instead of a lambda, so it no longer causes a parse error.

An annotation macro after the parameters of a function definition, such as "void f() const GTEST_LOCK_EXCLUDED_(mutex_) {", no longer causes a parse error in C++ files, also with a pointer or reference return type, in a class body, or with a qualified name as its argument.
A macro written without a comma between constructor initializers, such as ": a_(a), GTEST_DISABLE_MSC_WARNINGS_PUSH_(4355) b_(this)", no longer causes a parse error.
A macro that stands for the whole head of a for loop, such as "for All_children(root, node, "Para") {", no longer causes a parse error in C++ files.
Macros written before a call argument, such as "OpenFile(TESTFILEDIR TESTFILE)", no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.
A reference initialized with parentheses around a conditional expression, such as "const FilePath& path(a ? *this : b);", no longer causes a parse error.
Unnamed bit-fields such as "unsigned int : 0;" in a class or struct no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.
The C fixes (variables at an "@" address, "__asm { }" blocks, line markers inside declarations, casts with a macro after the star) also apply to C++ files.

An annotation macro after the parameters of a constructor or destructor definition, such as "ScopedTrace::~ScopedTrace() GTEST_LOCK_EXCLUDED_(&UnitTest::mutex_) {", no longer causes a parse error in C++ files.
Macro arguments that only a macro turning them into a string can take, such as "COU_ADD_SUITE(<suite_C>, ...)" and "COU_ADD_SUITE(C++Suite, ...)", no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.
Names with a byte that is not UTF-8 in them (a Latin-1 letter in a file saved as Latin-1) no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.

The interrupt, register bank, trap and alignment qualifiers of the Tasking compiler, such as void _interrupt(1) _bisr_(osdSystemLevel) osDispatcher(void) or T x __align(4);, no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.
The at-sign qualifiers of the Cosmic compiler, such as @interrupt void isr(void), no longer cause a parse error in C++ files.
A Ctrl-Z character, the end-of-file mark old DOS editors leave at the end of a file, no longer causes a parse error in C++ files.

In C++ files too, a function pointer parameter after a type name, such as uint16 f(uint8 (*const cb)(void));, a variable whose whole head is a macro call, an unnamed struct after memory class macros, a memory class macro before the star of a function name, one-line CodeWarrior assembly and an initializer value from an #include line no longer cause a parse error.

Added support for the modern CSS at-rules @container (including named containers and size, style and scroll-state queries), @layer (including lists and dotted names), @page (including :first, :left and :right) and @function.
Added support for CSS range-style media and container queries, such as (width < 600px) and (400px <= width <= 700px), and for if() conditions with media(), style() and supports() branches.
@import now accepts layer and layer(name) options and a supports() condition.
A last declaration without a closing semicolon, such as the content of an inline style attribute (a: b), is now read as a normal declaration instead of a broken selector.
Unquoted url() values, such as url(../a.png), url(#mask) and url(//cdn/x.woff), are now read correctly. Line-wrapped data URIs still work.
Escaped characters in ids and class names (#\31 23), identifiers with non-Latin characters, and line continuations inside strings are now handled correctly.

Added support for common real-world CSS: legacy *property hacks, "! important" with spaces or any letter case, attribute case flags ([a=b i]), fractional keyframe percentages, stray semicolons, and nested selectors with & after a descendant (b & {}).
Syntax highlighting now covers the new at-rules, container names, selector() in @supports, and the comparison operators in range queries.

Stylesheets copied out of HTML pages and Microsoft Word exports now parse: <!-- and --> between rules, <style> and </style> tags around the rules, at-rules such as @list l0:level1, and values that start with an escape, such as \F0B7 or \5B8B\4F53.
Minor fixes to make it compatible with latest Graft package
Plain backtick-quoted CSS blocks (with `${...}` placeholders inside) are now recognised as CSS on their own, including several blocks in one file.
`${...}` placeholders now work anywhere a value can appear, such as `border: 1px solid ${c}` or `margin: ${a} ${b}`. Before, they only worked as the first value of a declaration.
Placeholders can now be used as pseudo-class names, for example `a:${state} { ... }` or `&:${s} { ... }`, including when other pseudo-classes follow.
Declarations like `x: ${foo};` are no longer mistaken for nested selectors. This also fixes `:hover` rules that sit next to declarations containing placeholders.
CSS parsing now follows a newer CSS grammar version. This adds support for nested selectors that start with a combinator (such as `> .title` or `& + &`), `:has(...)` arguments, and `@scope` blocks.
CSS that sits inside an HTML style block now parses cleanly. The opening and closing style tags and the HTML comment markers around the CSS are recognised instead of being reported as errors.
At-rules can now take keywords with colon-separated prefixes, such as Tailwind-style "@apply hover:underline focus:outline-none". Several of these can be listed with commas.
Property values written with CSS escape sequences, such as icon-font codes like "content: \f101" or escaped font names, are now accepted as normal values instead of causing errors.
The ready-made Windows build has been rebuilt so it includes all of the changes above.
Generated parsers are now built for tree-sitter ABI 14 instead of ABI 15.
Negative numbers are now recognized in CSV, PSV and TSV files. Values such as -1, -2.3 and -0x1F are parsed as numbers or decimals instead of plain text.
The parsers for all three formats were regenerated with a newer version of the parser generator.

Typed and partially-typed destructuring declarations now parse — def (List diffs, Boolean isAncestor) = f() and mixed targets like def (Map cfg, opts, String name) = load(), both of which previously produced a MISSING ")" plus an ERROR node (grammar.js)
Destructuring_declaration exposes an optional repeatable type field accepting array_type, builtintype, identifier, qualified_type and type_with_generics (src/node-types.json)
The shipped prebuild was stale — a build reported 1 built while installing a byte-identical old binary, so the grammar change never reached graft's loaded parser
:: method reference operator now parses in every position — String::toUpperCase, obj::method, Foo::new, and in argument position — via a new method_reference rule (grammar.js)
As casts to a generic type now parse — x as Map<String, Object>, y as List<String> — via a new as_op rule whose right-hand side is a type rather than an expression (grammar.js)
Arrow lambdas now work as values and in both spellings — def f = x -> x + 1 and def f = (a, b) -> a <=> b; previously only the bare form in argument position parsed (grammar.js)
.@ and the other access operators are accepted as assignment targets — obj.@field = 5; reading already worked (grammar.js)

A bare lambda produced three empty lambda_expression nodes with no parameters child; it now yields one node with parameters and body, and the upstream expectation that encoded the broken shape was corrected

The prebuild was untracked — commit 7d94d1d recorded only the delete half of the earlier rename, leaving HEAD with no binding at all; restored and staged under the original name (prebuilds/win32-x64/@murtaza64+tree-sitter-groovy.node)
"as" removed from the binary_op operator table — x as T now yields an as_op node with value/type fields instead of a binary_op; the only shape change visible to consumers, and graft reads neither
Type_with_generics precedence raised to PREC.COMPARE + 1 so a generic argument list wins the shift against a < comparison — PREC.TOP was tried first and collided with new Type<T>(args)
The _bare_lambda alias was deleted and dropped from argument_list, now subsumed by the widened lambda_expression; a conflict declaration the regenerate flagged as unnecessary was also removed
Regression cases added in two new corpus files rather than extending upstream's, keeping merge surface minimal
Rebuilt the prebuilt Windows x64 native parser binary, with no grammar, source, test or query changes
Enum definitions are now recognized, including constants with arguments, constructors, fields, methods and `implements`.
Trait declarations are now recognized.
Static initializer blocks (`static { ... }`) inside classes are now recognized.
Constructors, with or without modifiers, are now recognized as methods of their class.

Nested annotations are now supported as annotation values (`schema = @Schema(...)`, `content = [@Content(...)]`, `@ApiResponses([...])`). Annotations and modifiers such as `final` are also accepted on method parameters.
Member access after a closure call, such as `xs.collect { it }.join(',')`, is now read as one chained call instead of being split into separate statements.
Slashy strings and regexes that contain a literal `$` (such as `/^\d+$/` or `/foo$/`) and empty slashy strings now parse correctly.

Several smaller Groovy forms now parse correctly: -- `throws` clauses -- generic superclasses -- interfaces extending several interfaces -- multiple `catch` blocks -- `for (final Type x in xs)` loops -- methods that use a modifier instead of a return type, such as `static sumAll(...)` -- `byte` type -- string-named method calls such as `get '/api/x'(...)` -- stars-only comments such as `/*****/`
Syntax highlighting now covers the `enum`, `trait`, `implements`, `throws` and `byte` keywords.
Java-style array creation with initial elements, such as `new byte[] { (byte)(v & 0xFF), 2 }`, no longer causes a parse error.

Methods with all-capitals parameter types (`AUTOSAR data`, `URI uri`, `T object`), capitalized method and parameter names, untyped constructor parameters and `def` followed by modifiers in any order (`def private f()`, `def static private f()`) now parse correctly.

Generic methods without a return type or after a modifier (`static <T> T f()`, `def <T> T f()`, `private <T extends EObject> T f()`), wildcard type arguments (`<? super A>`, `<? extends B>`) and method declarations in interfaces now parse correctly.
Try-with-resources (`try (Stream s = open()) { }`) and multi-catch (`catch (A | B e)`) are now recognized.

`instanceof` with a generic type, `as` with an all-capitals, generic or array type, casts to an all-capitals type parameter (`(T) object`) and array declarations (`String[] parts`) now parse correctly.
Number literals with a signed exponent (`1.5e-3`, `-1.79E+308`) now parse correctly.

Closure calls inside map values (`[a: xs.collect { it }.sort(), b: 1]`), calls in parenthesised map keys, assignments inside parentheses (`while ((line = r.readLine()) != null)`), method references called directly (`Integer::parseInt(s, 16)`), an index after a closure call and positional arguments before named ones now parse correctly.
A statement ending in a parenthesised expression, such as `int d = (int) (a / b)`, is no longer merged with the next line when that line starts with a name.
Jenkins pipeline blocks such as `stages { ... }` are no longer split into separate statements.
Slashy regexes with a backslash before an escaped slash (`/\*\\//`) no longer end too early and break the rest of the file.
Spock blocks with an empty label (`given:` right before `expect:`) now parse correctly.

An index such as `a[0]` used as a value or argument is now read as an index instead of a call with a list argument. With a space before the bracket (`a [0]`) it is still read as a call with a list argument.
`get '/api/x'(controller: 'x')` is now read as a call of `get` with the string-named call as its argument, instead of two separate statements.

Methods and fields whose type is written in capitals after a modifier or an annotation (`public T withName(String n)`, `private URI uri`, `@Override URI base()`), untyped fields after an access modifier alone (`private x = 1`) and type parameters bounded by an all-capitals type (`class Builder<T extends Builder>`, `class B<T extends B<T>>`) now parse correctly.
Class literals such as `Foo.class` and `String.class` now parse correctly.
`synchronized (lock) { ... }` blocks are now recognized, also with a class literal as the lock (`synchronized (Foo.class) { }`).
A triple-quoted string that starts with a line continuation (`'''\` at the end of the line) no longer causes a parse error in files with CRLF line endings.

Fields declared with `def` followed by modifiers (`def final static X = 1`, `def static String s`), `static def` fields holding closures, untyped fields with a capitalised name after modifiers (`static final RootFolder = 'x'`) and modifiers written before the access modifier (`final private Map<K, V> m`, `static protected void f()`, `abstract void run() public`) now parse correctly.
Declarations of several names, with or without values (`String a, b`, `String a = '', b = 'c'`, `int x = 0, y = 0` in a for loop), now parse as one declaration.
A for loop initialised by a plain assignment (`for (i = last; i > 0; i--)`) and a `return` on its own line followed by an assignment now parse correctly.

Command calls without parentheses used as values (`def r = f a: 1, b: 2, c: 3`, named arguments over several lines, `def r = f 1, 2, 3`), builder commands with a capitalised name and a string (`SandboxPath "${dir}"`), `void` as a closure body, Spock's `thrown Exception` (also before a `where:` label) and slashy strings with interpolation followed by a closure now parse correctly.
Closure parameters that mix typed and untyped names and default values (`{ String a = "", String b -> }`, `{ String a, b = 2 -> }`, `{ a, b = 2 -> }`) now parse correctly.

Additions, subtractions and multiplications written with spaces around the operator (`a + b`, `x - 1`, `n * 2`) are now read as binary operations instead of a command call with a signed argument, so `return a + b` and `x = a - b` no longer split into separate statements.

A line break now ends a statement before a line that starts with a name, a number or a string (`x = y` followed by `f(x)` on the next line), instead of reading the second line as an argument of the first. Lines that continue a statement (`else`, `catch`, `finally`, `in`, `as`, `instanceof`, `extends`, `implements`, `throws`, `while`) are not affected.

A call written right after a name inside call arguments, compound assignments used as arguments (`f(x += 1)`), generic methods without modifiers at the start of a line (`<T> T f()`) and for-each loops with an all-capitals type (`for (URI u in uris)`) now parse correctly.
Long chains of calls in deeply nested blocks no longer make the parser run out of memory or stop with an error.
The grammar now has an external scanner (`src/scanner.c`), compiled by the Node, Rust, Go, Swift and Python bindings.
Minor fixes to make it compatible with latest Graft package
Commit missing file

HTML comments are now recognized the way browsers read them, including the short forms "<!-->" and "<!--->" and the "--!>" ending. A comment with no ending now runs to the end of the file instead of causing a parse error.

A void element such as
, or now closes right away. Text, entities, comments and following elements that come after it are siblings, not children.
A plain ">" in text, such as "a > b" or "=>", is now read as normal text instead of producing a parse error.
Unquoted attribute values are more forgiving. Values that contain quotes, "=" or "<", such as id=a=b or href=foo"bar, are now accepted as one value.
Tag names that contain a dot, such as TYPO3 Fluid's <f:link.action> and some custom elements, are now parsed correctly.
The prebuilt Windows binary is no longer included in the package.

Documents whose last closing tag is cut off at the end of the file (for example a final "</html" with no ">", as some log generators write) now parse cleanly instead of producing an error, and every open element ends at the end of the file, the same way a browser reads it.

Damaged or truncated tag names, such as "<so...<" left behind when an export cut text short, are now read as a single tag name up to the next space, "/" or ">". Previously they split into a tag name plus a stray "<", which broke the structure of the rest of the document.
Stray "&" and "<" characters in normal text (like "a && b", "x <= y", "1<2", "<3") are now read as plain text, as browsers do, and no longer cause parse errors

Elements left open at the end of a file (for example "

a b" with no closing tags) are now closed automatically instead of being reported as errors
A start tag cut off by the end of the file (no closing ">") is now recognized, and its tag name and attributes are kept
Stray "/" characters inside a tag (like "<a / b>" or "<br / >") are ignored as browsers do, instead of breaking the tag
Attributes with an empty value after "=" (like "<a b=>") are now accepted, and values such as "a= b", "a==b" and "a=<b" are read the way browsers read them
Attribute names now follow browser rules more closely, so names containing "<" or quote characters (like "<a b\"c>") no longer cause errors
End tags with no open element, such as the that close a page footer kept in its own file, are now read as stray end tags, as browsers do, instead of causing parse errors

An <?xml ...?> declaration at the top of an XHTML page, and the <![if ...]> and <![endif]> markers that Microsoft Word writes, are now read as comments, as browsers do, instead of breaking the rest of the document

A stray quote after an attribute value, as in

, is now read as an attribute name, as browsers do, instead of causing a parse error

Trailing commas are now accepted at the end of arrays and objects (e.g. `[1, 2,]`), so JSON-with-comments files such as tsconfig.json and editor settings files are parsed without errors. An isolated comma such as `[,]` is still reported as an error.
A `\u` escape in a string must now be followed by exactly four hexadecimal digits, as the JSON standard requires. Previously a bare `\u` was accepted as valid.
The parser was regenerated with a newer version of the grammar tooling, and the test suite now covers trailing commas and `\u` escapes.

Strings with an unrecognised backslash sequence, such as unescaped Windows paths like "D:\Lib\x.c" or regex patterns like "\d", now parse as normal text and no longer break the whole document. Valid escapes like \n and \" are still highlighted as escapes, and an incomplete \u escape is still reported as an error.
Kotlin 2.2 context parameters are now recognized, including the older unnamed form such as "context(Type)". They also work in front of function types.
Explicit property backing fields ("field = ..." or "field: Type = ...") are now supported.
Kotlin script files, such as Gradle build scripts, can now place imports after other statements.
Guard conditions on "else" branches in "when" expressions are now supported ("else if <condition> ->").
Callable references on nullable types (for example "String?::plus") are now supported.
Single-line class bodies, such as "object Registry { fun register() {} }", and several declarations on one line now parse correctly.

Several constructs that were previously misread or broke the parse are now handled correctly. These are annotated function types ("@Composable () -> Unit"), constructor parameters named like soft keywords ("data", "value", "inner"), class headers whose constructor continues on the next line, and lambdas that start with a parenthesized expression or a single destructured parameter. The same fix covers block comments next to line breaks, and a leading ";" in a class body.

Syntax highlighting is better. It now covers the Any, Nothing, Unit and dynamic types, the "package", "by", "companion", "where" and "suspend" keywords, and callable references. Scope-aware (local variable) queries are also available.
Comments in Makefiles are now treated as ignorable "extra" elements in the syntax tree, so tools that use the parser can skip over them more reliably.
The parser has been regenerated with a newer version of the parser generator (0.27). This improves compatibility with current Tree-sitter tooling and editors.
Variable names built from other variables, such as `$(LIB)_FILES += a.c`, are now recognized as variable assignments.
Windows-style paths that use backslashes (e.g. `dir\make\file.mak`) are read as one word, and a backslash just before a variable reference (e.g. `$(DIR)\$(FILE)`) no longer breaks parsing.
`ifeq`/`ifneq` conditions in parentheses now accept arguments that contain spaces, `|`, and other free text, such as `ifneq ($(a) | $(b),$(c))`.
`ifdef (NAME)` and `ifndef (NAME)` with parentheses are now accepted and read the same as `ifdef NAME` and `ifndef NAME`.
Values and function arguments that contain balanced parentheses, such as `$(eval $(S)_OBJ:=(PATH))`, now parse without errors.
A function call line that ends with a stray semicolon or trailing spaces, such as `$(error ...);`, no longer causes a parse error.
Arguments of parenthesized `ifeq`/`ifneq` conditions now appear in the syntax tree as text instead of words or strings. Highlighting rules or queries that match the old structure may need updating.
A function call with an empty argument, such as `$(info )` to print an empty line, now parses without errors.
A variable value with a `)` that closes nothing, such as `P += -configuration $(ROOT))/../out`, is kept as text, as make does, instead of causing a parse error.
Override export VAR := value now parses.
The automatic variable $| (order-only prerequisites) is now recognized; before, a recipe that used it could make the whole file fail to parse.
Substitution references on automatic variables, such as $(^:c=o) or $(@:.mk=.m4), now parse.
A bare "else" followed by blanks before the end of the line no longer joins the next line's ifdef/ifeq into an "else ifdef", which left an endif over and caused a parse error.

Braces in variable names, targets and variable references, such as the {{{COMPONENT}}}_FLAGS := and $({{{COMPONENT}}}DIR) of makefile templates, are now accepted, as make does. ${VAR} references still work.
Parser generation now targets Tree-sitter language ABI 14 instead of 15, so the grammars work with older Tree-sitter runtimes.
The inline Markdown parser was regenerated with Tree-sitter v0.25.10 at ABI 14.
Emphasis next to numbers and underscores is now recognised correctly, for example _foobar1_ is shown as emphasis.
Nested bold and italic text is now handled correctly in mixed cases such as *foo**bar**baz*, *foo**bar*** and **foo*bar*baz**.

Code spans now close only on a backtick run of the same length as the opening one, and they no longer treat HTML tags inside them as markup. A longer dollar run inside a math span also no longer closes it early.
A code block whose closing fence is the last thing in the document, with no line break after it, is now closed properly.
Fence characters in the middle of a line no longer end a fenced code block early. Only a fence at the start of a line closes it.
Ordered lists can start at any number. Only a list starting with 1 can interrupt a paragraph, so lines like "2. text" after a paragraph stay plain text.
Headings and HTML comment blocks (such as "<!-->") that end at the very end of the document, or on their opening line, are now parsed correctly.

Tables now support empty cells (for example "||"), including rows with leading or trailing pipes. HTML entities and numeric character references are also highlighted, and the info string of a fenced code block is easier to access.
The MATLAB parser is now rebuilt in the older language format (version 14) with tree-sitter 0.25.10, so it loads in editors and tools that run older tree-sitter versions.
Make the generated Perl parser compatible with an older tree-sitter runtime. It now targets language ABI version 14 instead of 15.
Files with several heredocs (<<~EOF and similar) are now parsed correctly. Before, a later heredoc could wrongly take over the "indented" setting of the first one.
Parsing files with heredocs now uses less memory. Memory that was never released after parsing is now freed.
The parser now builds more reliably with newer compilers and tool versions. It also handles memory more safely.
"require" statements that load a file by path (a quoted string such as "$dir/Foo.pm" or a variable such as $file) are now recognized, as well as the existing form that takes a package name.
A here-document written right after a filehandle, as in print $fh <<EOT;, is now read correctly as a here-document instead of a left-shift operation. Real shifts such as $x << 2 still work as before.
Here-documents in files with Windows line endings (CRLF) are now read correctly. Before, the whole file could fail to parse.
Subroutine prototypes that contain a dollar sign, such as sub usage ($) { ... }, now parse; before, "$)" was read as a special variable.
Scalar names that start with an underscore, such as $_abc or $__CONFIG__DIR__, are now read as ordinary variables instead of $_ followed by a word.
Elements of a dereferenced array or hash, such as ${$ref}{key}, $$ref{key} and ${ \( shift ) }, now parse.
Switch ($x) { case 'A' { ... } else { ... } } blocks from the Switch module are now recognized.
Use statements with an import list of several items, such as use Test::More tests => 4;, now parse.
Empty statements, such as a doubled semicolon (use Foo;;) or a lone ; in a block, now parse.
Calls such as print normalizePath($_); are no longer read as a subroutine prototype.
The file glob operator, such as <*.pl> or <$dir/*.[ch]>, is now recognized.
Lists with empty elements between commas, such as ok($x, ,"msg"), now parse.
The repetition operator with a count of several digits, such as '-'x25, now parses, and subroutines named like x2 or x25 are read as names.
Key/value hash slices, such as %h{key}, now parse.
A transliteration with an escaped backslash right before the delimiter, such as tr|a\\||d, is now read correctly.

A here-document whose statement goes on after its body now parses, such as return <<EOT inside a subroutine with the closing } after the end word, or print $fh <<EOT without a semicolon on the same line. Before, the end word was reported as missing and the rest of the file failed to parse.

The process ID variable $$ before a closing bracket or an operator, such as if ($pid != $$) { ... }, is now read as a variable; before, it was read as a dereference that swallowed the rest of the statement. $$ followed by a name ($$ref) is still a dereference.
Variable attributes, such as my $count :shared;, are now recognized.
A bare function name before ->[ or ->{, such as shift->[0] or shift->{name}, now parses.
Bless with any reference expression, and with => before the class, such as bless $book->[$i] => $class, now parses.
Dereferences of a call with spaced arguments, such as %{shift @_} or @{foo $x}, and hash elements keyed by such a call, such as $can{lc $t}, now parse.
Hash slices with several keys, such as @h{'a', 'b'}, the main package variable form $::name, and globs named by an expression with a glob slot, such as *{"${class}::Fetch"}{CODE}, now parse.
Minor fixes to make it compatible with latest Graft package

Much broader PL/SQL syntax support. Anonymous DECLARE/BEGIN blocks, FORALL loops, XMLTABLE and JSON_TABLE, MULTISET operators, recursive queries with SEARCH and CYCLE, KEEP (DENSE_RANK) aggregates, interval and date literals, and q'[...]' quoted strings now parse correctly.

Support for database links (`table@remote_db`, `pkg.proc@remote_db(...)`), conditional compilation directives (`$IF ... $THEN`, `$$plsql_line`), SQL%BULK_ROWCOUNT and SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS, and the PL/SQL JSON object types.

Better handling of object types and triggers. Inheritance modifiers (NOT FINAL, NOT INSTANTIABLE, OVERRIDING), MAP and ORDER member functions, explicit SELF parameters, `(self AS Super).method()` calls, and INSTEAD OF triggers without FOR EACH ROW now parse.

Names that start with a keyword (LoopContacts, SetParamValue, LogMsg, newPeriod, groupFrom) are now read as one identifier instead of being split into a keyword plus a leftover. Identifiers with accented letters (such as "descripción") also work.
Fixed parsing of long dotted references (a.b.c.d), nested collection indexing (tab(i)(j)), empty argument lists (f()), and loop labels after END LOOP, EXIT, CONTINUE and GOTO.

Fixed parsing of conditions and expressions. This covers arithmetic inside comparisons, grouped AND/OR conditions, IN lists, tuple IN and = comparisons, quantified ANY/ALL comparisons, [NOT] EXISTS, LIKE ... ESCAPE, MEMBER OF, IS EMPTY, IS JSON, and window functions inside CASE.

SQL statements are covered more fully. UNION/INTERSECT/MINUS queries, parenthesized joins, inline views, MERGE with aliases, UPDATE and INSERT with alias-qualified columns, FOR UPDATE with ORDER BY, WHERE CURRENT OF, RETURNING ... BULK COLLECT, and %ROWTYPE declarations now parse.
Updated the parser generator tooling to a newer version, and the build now includes the new keyword scanner.
Minor fixes to make it compatible with latest Graft package
The prebuilt Windows parser binary is no longer included, so Windows users must build it locally.
The parser has been regenerated with a newer version of the Tree-sitter toolchain, which keeps it compatible with current Tree-sitter releases. The Razor syntax it recognizes is unchanged.
Sass maps such as `$m: (a: 1, "b": $c);` are now recognised, including a single pair and a trailing comma.
The `!default` and `!global` flags on variable assignments are now supported, alone or together.
`@use` now supports namespaces, for example `@use "x" as ns;` and `@use "x" as *;`.
`@include` now supports `using ($x)` content-block arguments, trailing commas, `$args...` and space-separated multi-value arguments. `@mixin` parameter lists now accept a trailing comma.

Selectors starting with a combinator in nested rules, such as `.a { > .b { ... } }`, are now supported. `@at-root` now accepts a selector such as `b#{&}`, and `@for ... to ...` (exclusive range) works alongside `through`.

Interpolation `#{...}` in property names, values and selectors is handled correctly. This fixes declarations such as `--#{$x}--left: var(--#{$y})` being mistaken for selectors, and covers nested interpolation and `a:#{$b};`.
Interpolated class names and identifiers now parse correctly when they continue with `_` or start with a digit, for example `.#{$x}__y` and `.#{$a}-500px`.

Bare escape sequences such as `$icon: \f42c;` are now recognised as values. Map keys such as `foo` in `(foo: 1)` no longer swallow the colon. Syntax highlighting now covers the CSS basics plus the new Sass constructs: flags, namespaces, `using`, `to` and escapes.
Processing instructions (such as <?php ... ?>) that span several lines, or that contain a "?" not followed by ">", are now read correctly instead of being cut off or rejected.
Entity declarations in a DTD can now contain markup characters like "<" in their values (for example bold">), as the XML specification allows.
Added test cases for multi-line processing instructions, markup inside entity values, and attribute values.
The parser sources were regenerated with a newer parser generator (tree-sitter-cli 0.27).

XML processing instructions (such as <?eclipse version="3.2"?>) now parse correctly when followed by Windows line endings, the end of the file, or more markup on the same line, so these files no longer show parse errors
Files longer than 32,767 lines now parse correctly to the end. Before, everything after that line was reported as an error.

Single-quoted text that continues over several lines now parses correctly when a continuation line is not indented further than the enclosing key. A typical case is a JSON blob in a Kubernetes annotation that closes with `]'` at the key's column.
Documents with very deep indentation no longer risk corrupted parser state or crashes when the parser saves and restores its position.
Saving and restoring parser state is now safe on platforms that need aligned memory access.
Added a test for multi-line single-quoted values in Kubernetes-style documents that contain several `---` separated documents.
